intro: A surveyor on the lakefront points a small instrument at the top of a building and reads an angle. A minute later she knows the building's height without touching it. A city engineer looks at the equation of a circle on a map and knows which homes a new cell tower will reach. A farmer orders a silo and needs to know, before it arrives, how many bushels it will hold. All three are using the same handful of ideas about shape and size, and all three ideas begin with a triangle you can measure standing in for one you cannot.

This unit starts with similarity: what it means for two figures to have the same shape, and the shortcuts that prove it. From similar right triangles come three ratios called sine, cosine and tangent, the tools that turn one angle and one side into every other part of a triangle. Then the circle takes over: the angles inside it, the arcs and sectors that make up its edge and interior, a new angle unit called the radian, and the equation that places a circle on a coordinate grid. The unit ends by stacking, slicing and comparing solids to find how much space a can, a cone, a pyramid or a ball takes up.

By the end you will be able to find a flagpole's height from its shadow, solve any right triangle from two of its parts, compute the area of a pizza slice or the length of a curved running track lane, write and read the equation of a circle, and find the volume and density of real objects modeled from simple solids. Every formula is built from a picture you can draw, and every method is checked on a real example first.
bigQuestion: How do ratios in one small triangle let us measure buildings, map circles and fill solids we can never take apart?

timeline.t: Thales of Miletus is credited with measuring a pyramid's height from its shadow using similar triangles
Euclid's Elements sets out similar triangles, circle theorems and a proof of the Pythagorean theorem
Archimedes shows a sphere holds two thirds of the cylinder that just contains it
Ptolemy's Almagest includes a table of chord lengths, an ancestor of trigonometric tables
Aryabhata in India tabulates half-chords, the idea that became the sine
European scholars gather trigonometry into a subject of its own for astronomy and navigation
Bonaventura Cavalieri publishes his method of comparing solids slice by slice
Descartes's La Géométrie links equations to curves, making the equation of a circle possible
William Jones first uses the symbol π for the ratio of circumference to diameter
The word radian enters mathematics textbooks as the natural unit of angle
The Americans with Disabilities Act leads to ramp standards with a maximum 1 to 12 slope, about 4.8°
Surveyors, GPS receivers and video-game engines all solve triangles millions of times a day

words.d: a transformation that multiplies every distance from a center point by the same scale factor
having the same shape: equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides
two triangles are similar if two angles of one equal two angles of the other
for an acute angle of a right triangle, opposite side divided by hypotenuse
for an acute angle of a right triangle, adjacent side divided by hypotenuse
for an acute angle of a right triangle, opposite side divided by adjacent side
the angle between the horizontal and a line of sight looking upward
an angle with its vertex on a circle; it measures half its intercepted arc
a line that touches a circle at exactly one point, perpendicular to the radius there
the angle whose arc equals the radius; a full circle is 2π radians
a wedge of a circle bounded by two radii and an arc; its area is (θ/360) × πr²
solids with equal heights and equal cross-section areas at every level have equal volumes

test.q: A dilation centered at the origin has scale factor 0.5. Where does (8, −6) land?
test.why: Multiply both coordinates by 0.5: (4, −3). Both coordinates change, not just x.

test.q: Two similar figures have scale factor 2. The larger figure's area is how many times the smaller's?
test.why: Area scales by the square of the scale factor: 2² = 4.

test.q: One triangle has angles 30° and 80°. Another has angles 70° and 80°. Are they similar?
choices: Yes, by AA, since the first triangle's third angle is 70°
No, because 30° is not in the second triangle
test.why: 180 − 30 − 80 = 70°, so both triangles have angles 30°, 70° and 80°. Two shared angles is AA.

test.q: A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. How long is the hypotenuse?
A 45-45-90 triangle has legs of 4. How long is the hypotenuse?
In a 5-12-13 right triangle, what is the sine of the angle across from the side of length 5?
test.why: Sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse = 5/13. The ratio 5/12 is the tangent.

test.q: A right triangle has legs 3 and 4. What is the angle across from the leg of length 3? Use tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.9°.
test.why: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent = 3/4 = 0.75, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.9°. The other acute angle is 53.1°.

test.q: From 100 m away, the angle of elevation to the top of a tower is 40°. How high is the top above eye level? Use tan 40° ≈ 0.839.
test.why: Height is opposite and 100 m is adjacent: height = 100 × 0.839 = 83.9 m. Dividing gives 119.2, the wrong direction.

test.q: A 1.8 m person casts a 3 m shadow while a tree casts a 15 m shadow. How tall is the tree?
test.why: Height ÷ shadow is 1.8/3 = 0.6 for both, so the tree is 15 × 0.6 = 9 m. Using 3/1.8 gives 25.

test.q: An inscribed angle measures 40°. What is the measure of its intercepted arc?
test.why: The arc is twice the inscribed angle: 2 × 40 = 80°.

test.q: A circle has radius 9. A point is 15 units from the center. How long is the tangent segment from the point to the circle?
test.why: Right triangle with hypotenuse 15 and leg 9: √(225 − 81) = √144 = 12.

test.q: A circle has radius 10. What is its circumference, to one decimal place?
test.why: C = 2πr = 20π ≈ 62.8. The value 314.2 is the area (100π).

test.q: A circle has radius 6. What is the length of a 120° arc, to one decimal place?
What are the center and radius of (x − 1)² + (y + 6)² = 16?
test.why: Flip the signs inside: center (1, −6). The radius is √16 = 4.

test.q: A cone has radius 2 cm and height 9 cm. What is its volume, to one decimal place?
test.why: V = (1/3) × π × 4 × 9 = 12π ≈ 37.7 cm³. The value 113.1 (36π) is the full cylinder.

write.prompt: A hiker stands 80 meters from the base of a cliff and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 38°. Her eyes are 1.6 meters above the ground. Find the height of the cliff and explain each step. Then explain a second way to find the height using only a shadow and a meter stick, and say which method you trust more and why.
tips: State your final answer with units before you explain.
Draw the right triangle and label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from the angle you use.
Show which ratio you chose and why, then show the multiplication or division.
Say whether you added the eye height, and why it matters.
Check your answer a second way, or explain what would make it wrong.
